explanation: New versions of the song have been tracked spreading eastward across the South Pacific, passed from one whale population to the next within a few years.

claims.text: Male humpback whales sing long, complex songs that they learn from one another and that change over time.
Blue whales, sperm whales and orcas do not sing long, complex songs that spread and change like humpback song.
New humpback song versions have spread eastward across the South Pacific from one population to the next within a few years.

writerNotes: Self-check (guide 9.3), all eleven codes confirmed true. The selfCheck field itself is left out because the CNT-1 item schema refuses it as an unknown key, so the codes are recorded here. lint: content:check reports no errors and no warnings for this item. claims: three listed; high: c3 (checker_doubt, raised by me because it rests on a specific study rather than textbook knowledge); standard: c1 and c2. datasets: no pinned dataset in content/datasets/manifest.json covers animal or plant biology (it holds countries, languages, currencies, cities, elements, Nobel Prizes, Olympic Games, World Cups, art collections and Natural Earth), so none applies, and the high-risk claims need web evidence from checker A; one search on humpback song spreading across the South Pacific should cover c3. rivalTest: Argued for the blue whale, which also sings, but in simple, repeated low calls rather than long, complex, learned songs. Sperm whales communicate in clicks and orcas in pod dialects, neither of them songs of this kind. volatility: evergreen, a settled fact that cannot change; no time words, and nothing rests on knowledge newer than mid-2026. regional: humpbacks live in every ocean and their song is famous worldwide. style: Oxford spelling, plain hyphens only, explanation of 26 words. myths: screened against content/reference/myths.json; no entry matches. mystery and encore: nothing of either kind in a multiple-choice item. doubts: c3 rests on one well-known study of South Pacific populations, so I raised it to high (checker_doubt).

evidence.restatement: Male humpback whales sing long, complex songs that they learn from one another and that change over time.
Blue whale songs are simple and repetitive, and sperm whales and orcas use clicks, codas and call dialects, not long complex songs that spread like humpback song.
New humpback song types have been tracked spreading eastward across the South Pacific, from eastern Australia to French Polynesia, within about two years.

Blue, sperm and killer whales do not sing complex songs that spread between populations and change like the humpback's.
New humpback song types have been tracked spreading eastward across the South Pacific, from one population to the next over a few years.
